chapterTitle: The Defense That Silenced Jerusalem and the Church That Got a Name
themeTitle: Who Was I, That I Could Withstand God?

scripture.text: Now the apostles and the brothers who were in Judea heard that the Gentiles had also received the word of God.
scripture.understanding: News travels faster than doctrine. Before Peter can even get home, word has run ahead of him: the outsiders — the uncircumcised — have received the same word of God the Jews received. The little word 'also' is the earthquake.

scripture.text: When Peter had come up to Jerusalem, those who were of the circumcision contended with him,
scripture.understanding: Peter walks into a headwind. 'Those of the circumcision' are not enemies of the gospel — they are believers who cannot yet imagine grace without the fence of the Law. The chief apostle is put on trial by his own church.

scripture.text: saying, “You went in to uncircumcised men, and ate with them!”
scripture.understanding: Notice the charge is not that Peter preached to Gentiles — it is that he ate with them. The table was the sacred boundary, the line no faithful Jew crossed. To share bread was to say: we are one people. That is what scandalized them.

scripture.text: But Peter began, and explained to them in order, saying,
scripture.understanding: Peter does not argue theology or pull rank. He simply tells the story 'in order' — step by step, exactly as it happened. When God has done something, the most powerful defense is a plain, honest account of what He did.

scripture.text: “I was in the city of Joppa praying, and in a trance I saw a vision: a certain container descending, like it was a great sheet let down from heaven by four corners. It came as far as me.
scripture.understanding: The revolution begins not in a strategy meeting but in prayer. Heaven itself lowers a sheet 'as far as me' — God stoops to Peter's exact position to overturn a boundary Peter thought was holy.

scripture.text: When I had looked intently at it, I considered, and saw the four-footed animals of the earth, wild animals, creeping things, and birds of the sky.
scripture.understanding: Peter looks 'intently' — this is no glance. The sheet holds every category of creature Leviticus had sorted into clean and unclean, all mixed together, all offered without distinction.

scripture.text: I also heard a voice saying to me, ‘Rise, Peter, kill and eat!’
scripture.understanding: The command is direct and shocking to a lifelong observant Jew: eat what your entire identity has trained you to refuse. God is dismantling a wall from the inside, one command at a time.

scripture.text: But I said, ‘Not so, Lord, for nothing unholy or unclean has ever entered into my mouth.’
scripture.understanding: 'Not so, Lord' — two words that cannot logically stand together. If He is Lord, there is no 'not so'; if you say 'not so,' He is not truly Lord. Peter's clean record becomes the very thing arguing against God.

scripture.text: But a voice answered me the second time out of heaven, ‘What God has cleansed, don’t you call unclean.’
scripture.understanding: This is the theological heart of the chapter. The issue was never the animals — it was the people they pictured. God has done the cleansing; man does not get to overrule the verdict of heaven.

scripture.text: This was done three times, and all were drawn up again into heaven.
scripture.understanding: Three times — the same emphatic repetition by which the Lord earlier restored Peter after three denials. God does not merely mention a truth to Peter; He drives it home until it cannot be dismissed as a passing thought.

scripture.text: Behold, immediately three men stood before the house where I was, having been sent from Caesarea to me.
scripture.understanding: The timing is not coincidence — it is choreography. The moment the vision ends, its meaning knocks at the door. God prepares the messenger and the message to arrive at the same instant.

scripture.text: The Spirit told me to go with them, without discriminating. These six brothers also accompanied me, and we entered into the man’s house.
scripture.understanding: The Holy Spirit is the true actor here. He commands Peter to go 'without discriminating' — making no distinction, no hesitation between Jew and Gentile. Peter brings six witnesses because he knows heaven is about to be doubted on earth.

scripture.text: He told us how he had seen the angel standing in his house, and saying to him, ‘Send to Joppa, and get Simon, who is called Peter,
scripture.understanding: God was working both ends at once. While He was preparing Peter with a vision, He was preparing Cornelius with an angel. Salvation is a divine appointment scheduled from both sides of the door.

scripture.text: who will speak to you words by which you will be saved, you and all your house.’
scripture.understanding: Even an angel does not preach the gospel — that privilege is given to human witnesses. Cornelius must hear 'words by which you will be saved.' Faith comes by hearing, and God will not bypass the spoken word.

scripture.text: As I began to speak, the Holy Spirit fell on them, even as on us at the beginning.
scripture.understanding: Peter barely gets started — 'as I began to speak' — and God interrupts the sermon with Pentecost. 'Even as on us at the beginning' means the Gentiles received the identical gift. Heaven refused to make them second-class.

scripture.text: I remembered the word of the Lord, how he said, ‘John indeed baptized in water, but you will be baptized in the Holy Spirit.’
scripture.understanding: The Spirit falling makes Peter remember the Lord's own promise. What happened in that Gentile house was not an anomaly — it was Jesus keeping His word. Experience and Scripture confirmed each other.

scripture.text: If then God gave to them the same gift as us, when we believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I, that I could withstand God?”
scripture.understanding: This is the sentence that ends the argument. Peter does not defend himself; he confesses his smallness. If God has already given the gift, resisting is not caution — it is fighting God Himself. The 'same gift' erases every distinction of birth.

scripture.text: When they heard these things, they held their peace, and glorified God, saying, “Then God has also granted to the Gentiles repentance to life!”
scripture.understanding: The critics fall silent, then worship. This is the verdict of the Jerusalem church: repentance itself is a gift 'granted' by God, and He has now granted it to the Gentiles unto life. The door is officially, publicly open.

scripture.text: They therefore who were scattered abroad by the oppression that arose about Stephen traveled as far as Phoenicia, Cyprus, and Antioch, speaking the word to no one except to Jews only.
scripture.understanding: Luke rewinds to the persecution that killed Stephen. What looked like the crushing of the church was actually its scattering like seed. The blood of the first martyr became the mission's launch — though at first still only to Jews.

scripture.text: But there were some of them, men of Cyprus and Cyrene, who, when they had come to Antioch, spoke to the Hellenists, preaching the Lord Jesus.
scripture.understanding: History turns on unnamed men. These anonymous believers from Cyprus and Cyrene did what the apostles had not yet dared — they preached the good news of Jesus to Greeks. The great Gentile mission began with people whose names we do not even know.

scripture.text: The hand of the Lord was with them, and a great number believed and turned to the Lord.
scripture.understanding: Their courage met God's power — 'the hand of the Lord was with them.' The result was not a trickle but a 'great number' who believed and turned. Antioch becomes the launching pad of the Gentile church.

scripture.text: The report concerning them came to the ears of the assembly which was in Jerusalem. They sent out Barnabas to go as far as Antioch,
scripture.understanding: Jerusalem sends a man to inspect the new thing — and mercifully, they send Barnabas, the 'son of encouragement.' The right man makes all the difference; a suspicious critic could have quenched what God was igniting.

scripture.text: who, when he had come, and had seen the grace of God, was glad. He exhorted them all, that with purpose of heart they should remain near to the Lord.
scripture.understanding: Barnabas does not test their pedigree; he 'sees the grace of God' and rejoices. His counsel is simple and durable: with settled purpose of heart, stay close to the Lord. Grace once received must be clung to.

scripture.text: For he was a good man, and full of the Holy Spirit and of faith, and many people were added to the Lord.
scripture.understanding: Luke pauses to praise Barnabas: good, Spirit-filled, full of faith. And note the fruit — 'many people were added to the Lord.' A generous, encouraging, Spirit-filled character is itself a soul-winning force.

scripture.text: Barnabas went out to Tarsus to look for Saul.
scripture.understanding: Barnabas cannot handle the harvest alone, so he goes hunting for the one man everyone else still feared — Saul of Tarsus. The encourager remembers the convert nobody trusted and pulls him into the front line of the mission.

scripture.text: When he had found him, he brought him to Antioch. For a whole year they were gathered together with the assembly, and taught many people. The disciples were first called Christians in Antioch.
scripture.understanding: A full year of steady teaching produces something new under heaven: the watching city gives the disciples a name — 'Christians,' the Christ-people. Their lives had become so saturated with Jesus that outsiders named them after Him.

scripture.text: Now in these days, prophets came down from Jerusalem to Antioch.
scripture.understanding: The traffic that once ran only from Jerusalem outward now flows back and forth — Jerusalem sends prophets down to the young Gentile church. The two communities are already bound together as one body.

scripture.text: One of them named Agabus stood up, and indicated by the Spirit that there should be a great famine all over the world, which also happened in the days of Claudius.
scripture.understanding: The same Spirit who fell on Cornelius now speaks a warning through Agabus. Luke confirms it came true under Claudius — genuine prophecy, historically verified. God warns His people in advance so love can prepare a response.

scripture.text: As any of the disciples had plenty, each determined to send relief to the brothers who lived in Judea;
scripture.understanding: The Gentile church's first instinct, on hearing of coming hardship, is to give. Each gives 'as he had plenty' — proportional, willing, personal. The ones Jerusalem had suspected now become Jerusalem's providers.

scripture.text: which they also did, sending it to the elders by the hands of Barnabas and Saul.
scripture.understanding: They did not merely intend to help — 'which they also did.' The gift travels by the hands of Barnabas and Saul, and the gospel's fruit is proven: Gentile money crossing the very line the circumcision party had defended, to feed Jewish believers in need.

visualMeditations.title: The Sheet Let Down From Heaven
visualMeditations.image: Picture Peter on a flat rooftop in Joppa, hungry and praying under the noon sun, when the sky seems to open and a vast linen sheet, knotted at its four corners, is lowered slowly toward him — 'as far as me,' he says. And crawling and slithering and flapping inside it is every kind of creature: cattle and wild beasts, lizards and snakes, hawks and crows — the clean and the unclean piled together in one bundle, all being handed to him as food.
visualMeditations.meaning: For a Jew, the food laws were not a diet — they were a fence around identity, a daily, edible reminder that Israel was a separated people. In that sheet God is not fussing about menus; He is folding the whole clean/unclean system into one bundle and offering it back cleansed. The animals were a parable, and the punchline was people: the Gentiles Peter had been trained to keep at arm's length.

visualMeditations.title: The Same Gift, the Same Beginning
visualMeditations.image: Peter opens his mouth in Cornelius' Gentile house — he has barely gotten a sentence out — and heaven crashes the meeting. The Holy Spirit falls on that roomful of uncircumcised Romans exactly as He had fallen on the hundred and twenty in the upper room at Pentecost. Same wind, same fire, same overflowing tongues. Peter freezes mid-sermon, watching Pentecost happen all over again in the last place he expected it.
visualMeditations.meaning: God did not give the Gentiles a lesser, second-tier Spirit. Peter's word is precise: 'even as on us at the beginning.' The gift was identical, which meant the recipients were equal. Heaven had already made the decision Jerusalem was still arguing about; God baptized the Gentiles before any human council could vote on whether He was allowed to.

visualMeditations.title: The Hand of the Lord at Antioch
visualMeditations.image: In the great cosmopolitan city of Antioch — a swirl of Greeks, Syrians, Romans and every idol in the empire — a handful of no-name refugees from Cyprus and Cyrene start telling strangers about a crucified and risen Jew named Jesus. And an unseen hand rests on the whole effort. Not the hand of a strategy, not the hand of the apostles, but 'the hand of the Lord.' The crowd does not merely nod; a great number turn all the way around and face a new Master.
visualMeditations.meaning: The Gentile mission's first great breakthrough came without an apostle present and without a single famous name attached. It came because the hand of the Lord was on ordinary, obedient people. When God's hand is on the work, unnamed messengers turn a pagan metropolis, and the church discovers that its power was never its platform — it was His presence.

visualMeditations.title: The Disciples Called Christians
visualMeditations.image: For a whole year Barnabas and Saul teach in Antioch, and the disciples become impossible to ignore — a people whose speech, whose generosity, whose whole lives keep circling back to one name: Christ. Finally the outsiders coin a label for them, half description and half nickname: Christianoi — 'Christ's people,' 'the Christ-ones.' They did not choose the name for themselves. The city fastened it on them because it fit.
visualMeditations.meaning: A name given by outsiders is a verdict on your life. Antioch's pagans could not describe these people without reaching for the name of Jesus, because Jesus was the most obvious thing about them. The label that would one day be worn by martyrs and inscribed on the whole global church was born in a Gentile city, as a description of lives so saturated with Christ that His name became their name.

structure.label: The Circumcision Party's Charge (v. 1-3)
structure.body: Peter is summoned before the Jerusalem believers and accused — not of preaching to Gentiles, but of eating with them and crossing the sacred boundary of the table.

structure.label: Peter's Orderly Defense (v. 4-17)
structure.body: Peter answers not with argument but with narrative, retelling the vision at Joppa, the Spirit's command to go without distinction, and the Spirit falling on the Gentiles exactly as at Pentecost.

structure.label: Jerusalem Silenced and Glorifying God (v. 18)
structure.body: The critics fall silent and then worship, confessing that God Himself has granted repentance to life to the Gentiles.

structure.label: The Gospel Leaps to Antioch (v. 19-21)
structure.body: The scattering after Stephen's death carries the word to Antioch, where unnamed men preach to Greeks and a great number turn to the Lord under the hand of God.

structure.label: Barnabas, Saul, and a New Name (v. 22-26)
structure.body: Jerusalem sends Barnabas, who fetches Saul from Tarsus; a year of teaching produces a church so marked by Christ that the city names them 'Christians.'

structure.label: Famine Foretold and Relief Sent (v. 27-30)
structure.body: The prophet Agabus foretells a worldwide famine, and the young Gentile church responds by sending relief to the Jewish believers in Judea by the hands of Barnabas and Saul.

sections.heading: The Battle Over the Table
paragraphs: Understand what is actually on trial in the first eighteen verses, because it is not what we assume. The circumcision party does not accuse Peter of preaching salvation to Gentiles — that alone might have been tolerated at a safe distance. Their exact charge is, 'You went in to uncircumcised men, and ate with them!' The scandal is table fellowship. In that world the shared meal was a covenant act; to eat together was to declare, before God and man, 'we are one people, we belong to the same family.' The food laws had built a wall precisely to keep that from happening across the Jew-Gentile line. Peter had walked straight through the wall.

This is the first great internal crisis of the church, and it is a battle over grace itself. Can a person belong fully to God without first belonging to the fence of the Law? The whole gospel hangs on the answer. If the Gentiles must first become Jews to become Christians, then salvation is by works of the Law after all, and the cross is not enough. Peter's defense is devastating precisely because he takes no credit and offers no clever argument — he simply testifies to what God did, and lands on the one sentence no believer can answer: 'who was I, that I could withstand God?' You cannot fight a God who has already handed out the gift. When heaven has already decided, human objection is not piety — it is resistance to God.

sections.heading: What God Has Cleansed
paragraphs: The hinge of the entire chapter is the voice from heaven in verse 9: 'What God has cleansed, don't you call unclean.' Peter's whole identity had been built on the ability to sort the world into clean and unclean, holy and common, us and them. God does not tell Peter to relax his standards; He tells Peter that the standard-setter has already run the cleansing and the verdict is final. The uncleanness Peter still felt toward the Gentiles was now a private opinion in defiance of a divine decree. This is why Peter can go 'without discriminating' (v. 12) — the Greek word means to make no distinction, to withdraw no fellowship. The dividing line was not softened; it was abolished at the source, by the blood that cleanses.

And then, having settled the doctrine, Luke immediately shows the doctrine walking. The famine relief of verses 27–30 is the theology of verse 9 in action. The very Gentile believers whom the circumcision party had suspected of being unclean now empty their pockets to feed the Jewish believers in Judea. Grace flowed one direction — Jew to Gentile — through Peter's door; now love flows the other direction — Gentile to Jew — through the hands of Barnabas and Saul. The wall did not merely come down; traffic now runs across the rubble in both directions. That is the shape of the true church: no distinction in cleansing, and no distinction in love.

ntConnection.heading: New Testament Connection
paragraphs: Peter's testimony in this chapter was not a one-time speech — it became the decisive argument that settled the future of the whole church. Years later, when the same question exploded into the Jerusalem Council of Acts 15, Peter stood up and appealed to exactly this event: 'God, who knows the heart, testified about them, giving them the Holy Spirit, just like he did to us. He made no distinction between us and them, cleansing their hearts by faith' (Acts 15:8-9). Read those words against Acts 11 and the connection is unmistakable: the 'same gift' Peter saw fall (11:15-17), the 'without discriminating' the Spirit commanded (11:12), and the cleansing voice from heaven (11:9) are all gathered up and turned into official doctrine — God makes no distinction, and He cleanses hearts by faith alone. The story of Acts 11 becomes the theology of Acts 15.

There is also a piercing sequel to Peter's stand. Here in chapter 11 Peter is the hero who dares to eat with Gentiles; but Paul later records in Galatians 2:11-14 that this same Peter, back in this same Antioch, one day 'drew back and separated himself' from Gentile tables out of fear of the circumcision party — and Paul 'resisted him to his face, because he stood condemned.' The man who once asked 'who was I, that I could withstand God?' had to be reminded not to withstand the very gospel he had defended. And the name born here — 'Christians' — reappears in the mouth of the apostle Peter himself: 'if one of you suffers for being a Christian, let him not be ashamed; but let him glorify God in this matter' (1 Peter 4:16). The nickname the pagans of Antioch coined became the honored name under which the church would suffer, glorify God, and conquer the world.

lexicon.insight: To make clean, to purify, to declare pure. The voice from heaven says, 'What God has cleansed, don't you call unclean.' The verb is decisive and completed — God has already done the purifying. The whole clean/unclean system of Leviticus is not being ignored but fulfilled: the true cleansing was never in the diet, it was in the heart, and God has now applied it to Gentiles. Peter's continued sense of their uncleanness had become a human opinion overruled by a divine act.

Literally to separate thoroughly, to make a distinction, to judge between, and so also to waver or hesitate. The Spirit tells Peter to go with the Gentile messengers 'without discriminating' — making no distinction between clean and unclean, us and them, and not hesitating for a moment. This single word carries the chapter's revolution: the ancient dividing line between Jew and Gentile is not to be honored, weighed, or debated but crossed without a second thought, because the Spirit Himself commands it.

A change of mind, a turning of the whole inner direction, from the verb 'to think differently afterward.' The Jerusalem church confesses that 'God has also granted to the Gentiles repentance to life.' Notice it is granted — repentance itself is a gift God gives, not merely a human achievement. And it is 'to life': this change of mind opens into eternal life. The critics realize that if God is handing out repentance to Gentiles, the argument is over, and worship is the only fitting response.

To turn around, to turn back, to convert — a decisive change of direction. At Antioch 'a great number believed and turned to the Lord.' The word pairs belief with a physical about-face: real faith is not merely agreeing but wheeling the whole life around to face a new Master. It is the same movement the prophets begged Israel to make, now happening spontaneously among pagan Greeks under the hand of the Lord — proof that the gospel had truly leapt the Jewish boundary.

'Christ-people,' followers of Christ — the name given to the disciples first at Antioch. The verb translated 'were called' is chrēmatízō (G5537), a striking word that means to be divinely named, to bear a title, even to be given an oracle. Though the label came from watching outsiders, Luke's word hints it was more than a nickname — it was a name that stuck by the hand of providence. These believers were so saturated with Christ that the city could not describe them without His name. The label born here would one day be worn by martyrs and inscribed on the whole global church.

holySpiritRevelation.intro: The Spirit is dealing with the lines you have quietly drawn in the name of holiness — the people, the tables, the categories you have filed away as 'unclean,' and the places where your caution has actually become resistance to God.

items.title: The Question That Ends Every Argument
items.body: Peter's whole defense collapses into one sentence: 'Who was I, that I could withstand God?' There is a kind of resistance that dresses itself up as reverence — 'Not so, Lord' — but two words that cannot stand together. If He is Lord, there is no 'not so.' Where in your life are you still saying 'Not so, Lord' about a person, a call, or a change He has clearly initiated? Has your carefulness quietly become a way of withstanding God? What would it cost you today to stop defending yourself and simply confess your smallness before what He has already done?

items.title: What God Has Cleansed, Stop Calling Unclean
items.body: The voice from heaven did not lower God's standard; it announced that God had already met it. There are people you have written off, categories you have quietly excluded, and perhaps a version of yourself you keep labeling 'unclean' long after the blood of Jesus declared otherwise. Whose name have you struck off your list that heaven has already added? And what about you — do you keep calling unclean the very heart God has cleansed, refusing to believe grace could reach that deep? Who told you to keep the fence God has already torn down?

items.title: Named After the One You Love
items.body: The disciples did not call themselves Christians; the city did, because Jesus was the most obvious thing about them. A name given by outsiders is a verdict on your life. If the people who watch you all week had to coin a one-word label for you based only on what your mouth, your money, and your habits keep circling back to — what name would they reach for? Would it be His? What in your life would have to change this week for the watching world to be unable to describe you without the name of Christ?

audit.title: The 'Uncircumcised Table' Check
audit.body: The charge against Peter was not what he preached but who he ate with. Who is the person or group you would rather keep at arm's length — a different class, culture, past, or politics — whom you have never actually invited to your table? Have you mistaken your comfort for holiness?

audit.title: The 'Withstand God' Audit
audit.body: Where in your life is God clearly opening a door while you keep politely saying 'Not so, Lord'? Name the thing you are resisting under the cover of caution or tradition. Is it possible that the very carefulness you are proud of is actually you withstanding God?

audit.title: The 'Christian' Test
audit.body: The name was given by watchers, not chosen by the disciples. If the coworkers, neighbors, and strangers who observe your ordinary week had to name you by what your life keeps pointing to, would 'Christ-person' honestly fit? Or would the label they reach for be something else entirely?

practices.title: Cross One Table This Week
practices.body: Identify one person you have quietly filed under 'not my kind' — and this week deliberately share a meal, a coffee, or a real conversation with them. Do the concrete thing Peter was accused of. Before you go, pray Peter's confession: 'Who am I, that I could withstand God?' Let the table itself preach that God makes no distinction.

practices.title: Send Relief Like Antioch
practices.body: The young Gentile church heard of coming hardship and immediately gave, 'each as he had plenty.' Pick one real need you know of — a struggling family, a believer in a hard place, a genuine ministry — and this week send tangible relief in proportion to what you have. Do not merely intend it, as Antioch did not merely intend it: 'which they also did.' Give it by your own hands.

prayerReflection: "Lord Jesus, I confess how often I have said 'Not so, Lord' to the very things You were commanding — how I have dressed up my resistance as reverence and called my comfort holiness. Forgive me for the lines I have drawn around people You have already cleansed, and for calling unclean what the heaven of Your grace has washed. Who am I, that I could withstand You? Give me the humility of Peter, who stopped defending himself and simply told the truth of what You had done. Put Your hand upon me as it was upon the men at Antioch, so that my ordinary obedience turns hearts to You. Grant me repentance that leads to life, and grant it freely to those I had written off. Make my life so full of Your Holy Spirit and of faith, like Barnabas, that the watching world cannot describe me without reaching for Your name. And when I see a brother in need, let me not merely intend to help but do it, by my own hands, sending relief across every line the fear of man has ever drawn. Let me be worthy of the name they first spoke at Antioch — a Christian, one of Yours. In Jesus' name, Amen."

storyConnections.title: Peter at Cornelius' House
storyConnections.summary: Acts 11 is Peter's own retelling of what actually happened in the previous chapter. In Acts 10, a devout Roman centurion named Cornelius is told by an angel to send for Peter, while Peter simultaneously receives the vision of the sheet three times on a Joppa rooftop. When Peter finally preaches in Cornelius' Gentile home, the Holy Spirit falls on the whole household before he even finishes, and Peter baptizes them. Chapter 11 shows the aftershock: the moment word reaches Jerusalem, Peter must defend the whole thing — proving that God's crossing of the Jew-Gentile line was so unprecedented it needed both a divine act and a public defense to be believed.

storyConnections.title: Jonah and the Mercy He Resisted
storyConnections.summary: Peter's 'Not so, Lord' echoes an older prophet's rebellion. Jonah was sent to preach to the pagan Gentiles of Nineveh and fled in the opposite direction, because he could not stomach the thought of God's mercy reaching Israel's enemies. When Nineveh repented and God relented, Jonah sulked in anger. Peter stands at the same crossroads on the Joppa rooftop — and the coast of Joppa is the very port from which Jonah once sailed away from God's call to the Gentiles. But this time the apostle lets God overrule his objection, goes to the Gentiles, and rejoices when 'God has also granted to the Gentiles repentance to life.' Peter becomes the Jonah who finally obeyed.

storyConnections.title: Joseph and Bread in the Famine
storyConnections.summary: When Agabus foretells a great famine and the Antioch church sends relief to Judea, they walk in an ancient pattern. Generations earlier, God warned Pharaoh through Joseph of seven years of famine, and Joseph stored grain so that when the famine came, there was bread for the world — and specifically for his own estranged brothers who had once sold him. In both stories God gives advance warning of famine so that His people can prepare provision, and in both the provision crosses a wounded relationship: Joseph feeds the brothers who betrayed him, and the Gentile believers feed the Jewish believers who had doubted them. God turns foreknowledge of hardship into an occasion for reconciling love.
